note: Every entry names where it was shown. On chain means a transaction on Cardano preprod; evaluation means the node provider ran the validator on a transaction that was never sent; tests means a contract test in CI.

first.note: had the double-satisfaction flaw; kept as evidence

items.claim: One validator checks the signer, the request, the age and the rule, then pays the beneficiary. 78 contract tests pass, including the four tamper cases API3 asks for.
items.detail: Current validator, script hash 58fb7eef. CI run 41090389165.

items.claim: We attacked our own first version and found a real flaw: two policies with the same beneficiary could be released with one payment, and the submitter kept the second payout. The fix allows one policy per release and the same attack is now refused.
items.detail: Same response, same wallet, same transaction: ACCEPTED by the first validator, REJECTED by the current one. Nothing was sent.

items.claim: A buyer's x402 payment goes straight into the validator with the policy as its datum (Cardano's script transfer method).
items.detail: Current validator: 5 tADA payment, HTTP 200 after 52 s; the client first recomputed the whole datum and found it matched.

items.claim: The seller's own keeper found that escrow and released it about 40 seconds later with no further command. 5 tADA reached the seller; the observation-time check passed on chain.
items.detail: Current validator. The keeper finds policies that pay it, fetches a signed price, checks it and releases.

items.claim: The refund works: a refund 343 seconds before the deadline was refused by the validator, and after the deadline the buyer got the money back.
items.detail: First validator; the refund code path is unchanged in the current one. The early refund was an evaluation.

items.claim: A paid keeper job: the buyer pays 2 tADA by x402, and is charged only if the keeper releases. A refused request left both balances unchanged.
items.detail: First validator. HTTP 200 after 91 s; a request for the wrong source returned 422 and charged nothing.

items.claim: The very first paid x402 request on Cardano preprod (the Cardano track's gate), through the official template.
items.detail: A placeholder route; it proved the facilitator and our wallets work.

items.claim: A real signed Open-Meteo rainfall response (14 daily values for Munich, sum 26.2 mm) released a policy that pays below 30 mm.
items.detail: First validator.

items.claim: A response signed 16 seconds earlier released a policy that accepts only 5 minutes: the age limit really binds.
items.detail: First validator. 0.1 aUSD paid on Base Sepolia for the fresh response.

items.claim: The same contract, a second industry: a signed tweet response (likes) released a Creator Pay policy; an edited count and an unmet KPI were refused.
items.detail: First validator; the contract was not changed for it.

items.claim: The keeper agent: scheduled cycles, a spending cap, backoff after failures and a log line per cycle. Two releases, and one run that waited 22 cycles through three failed fetches without releasing, as it should.
items.detail: First validator, free Nodary price data.

items.claim: A view count of a YouTube video, signed by the LunarCrush Airnode, passes the same validator logic: 8 tests with the real response (views 1,090,232; an edited count, another video's request, a wrong signer and a stale response are refused). It is not offered as a service template yet.
items.detail: The request asks the Airnode to project the post to {comments, id, likes, views}, so the signed text is 66 bytes and carries the video id. Limits: LunarCrush only holds posts it indexes, and the same video showed exactly the same counts 7 hours apart, so these are snapshots, not a live counter. Instagram was only listed (150 posts of one account), not tested against the contract.

items.claim: Three kinds of outcome run through the same contract and the same paid route: the likes of a tweet, Munich rainfall, and (as a free test fixture, not a use case) a price feed. Each was an x402 payment into the validator followed by a release by the seller's keeper, with its own signed data and no contract change.
items.detail: Tweet 20 at least 300,000 likes (308,791 seen, 0.01 aUSD), rainfall below 30 mm (26.2 mm seen, 0.1 aUSD), and the price fixture (free). The like count had fallen since an earlier test, so likes are not monotonic.

items.claim: Run from the console: an escrow that nobody can release was paid, an early refund was refused by the contract, and after the deadline the buyer's key refunded it.
items.detail: Current validator, from the "Run it live" panel.

items.claim: A like on a post paid out on chain: 5 tADA locked by x402 for "likes of the post at least 1", a like clicked at 18:22:46, the keeper saw it in 6 s and the release was on chain 53 s after the like (about 47 s of that is the chain). The rule came from the generic source tool, not from a hand-built template.
items.detail: The signed like count followed a like within the next response (about 2 s) in two timed runs. The beneficiary was the team's own seller key, so only fees were spent. Not tested: several likers at once or a judge's phone.

items.claim: A creator campaign paid in tranches, on chain: the campaign part was paid to a named payee (not the seller) after its measurement window opened; the retention part, measured later when the post was no longer liked, was not paid and was refunded to the buyer after its deadline.
items.detail: Three escrows on one post, with the author, creation time, id and exact text pinned in the signed text. The keeper made no paid check before a window opened. The deletion was simulated by unliking, the post was not deleted. The payee was the team's own buyer wallet.

items.claim: The seller's keeper released our own standing judge bench: it names the seller as beneficiary and pins a request the keeper had just learned to prove. The bench now names the buyer's key. We also fixed a wasted paid fetch and a provider call that could hang.
items.detail: Two releases of 5 tADA to our own seller key, 0.2 aUSD spent. Nothing was lost but the bench, which was re-locked.

items.claim: The seller's keeper survived injected failures, three escrows at once, a buyer who was told the payment had failed when it had not, and a crash right after a release was sent. All three escrows were released, once each, and the restarted keeper found the open ones again from the chain with no saved state.
items.detail: Two cycle faults, two fetch faults and one blind-evaluator fault were injected on purpose; the service was killed before the first release was confirmed.

items.claim: The seller's keeper does not poll a paid source on a timer. It plans each check from the cost, the kind of data and the last values: rainfall over a finished window was paid for once, the likes of a tweet three times at gaps it worked out (2, 3.2 and then 15 minutes, the last one past its stop time), 0.13 aUSD in all for two escrows that could never be released.
items.detail: Two escrows with unreachable rules were paid by x402 into the validator, left to the keeper and refunded after the deadline. The rule, a simulation against checking every minute and every five minutes, and the limits (invented histories, a crude two-point trend, no measured price of delay) are in POLLING.md.

items.claim: The tamper bench: one real response is accepted, and an edited value, a stale response, a response to a different request and a foreign signer are all refused. Run it on the Tamper bench tab.
items.detail: Six steps with a control before and after. The bench policies are locked on the current validator.

items.claim: Nobody can redirect the money: releasing without paying the beneficiary, paying an attacker, or underpaying by one lovelace are all refused; wrong refunders (no signer, an attacker, the beneficiary) are refused.
items.detail: Thirteen release cases and five refund cases, controls first and last. Anyone may submit a correct release.

items.claim: A lying seller cannot slip a bad datum past the buyer: the client recomputes the whole policy and refuses on any difference. 54 dishonest price lists over three templates, all refused.
items.detail: The facilitator does not look at the datum, so this check is the buyer's last line of defence.

items.claim: A public judge site (https://pay-on-proof-judge.vercel.app) runs the tamper bench for anyone, with no key on the host: 6 of 6 cases came out as expected against the live validator (control accepted, four tampered cases rejected, control accepted).
items.detail: The site uses an address-only client and never sends a transaction; a verdict is the node's script evaluation of an unsigned release. Not load tested.

items.claim: An AI agent can use the contract through seven tools (MCP): read what is locked, preview a payment, ask the validator for a verdict. The test client got ACCEPTED for the real response and REJECTED for one with an edited value, and both spending tools refused while spending was off (14 of 14 checks).
items.detail: Spending (5 tADA by x402) is off unless the operator enables it, then every call needs confirmation. Not tried in a real Claude Desktop session.

items.claim: The provider being unreachable for minutes, the facilitator being down, a rule-not-met case on the escrow route, a stale observation on chain, and a public judge URL.
items.detail: On the build list. (The three templates are shown above.)

items.claim: A signature proves what the API returned, not that it is true. There is no dispute process. Observation time is checked only for feeds that sign one (the Nodary price). Not audited.
items.detail: These are limits, not tasks. See TRUST.md.
